title: Respiratory System Examination
subtitle: A step-by-step practical guide to inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation
examInstructions: Choose the best answer for each station-style question. Select an option to reveal feedback.

pages.title: Preparation and patient positioning
pages.intro: Begin with a structured approach. Confirm the patient's identity, explain the examination, obtain consent, and ensure adequate exposure while maintaining dignity.

blocks.title: Before you begin
items: Perform hand hygiene and introduce yourself.
Confirm identity and explain what the examination involves.
Obtain consent and ask about pain before touching the patient.
Position the patient sitting upright and expose the chest appropriately.
Compare corresponding areas on the left and right sides.

blocks.title: Clinical note
blocks.text: If the patient becomes breathless or distressed, pause the examination and assess their immediate clinical needs.

images.title: Patient position
images.alt: Placeholder for an illustration of a patient sitting upright for a respiratory examination
images.caption: Insert a positioning photograph or labelled clinical illustration here.
images.explanation: The patient should be comfortably seated with the chest accessible. Preserve privacy and expose only the area required for each examination step.

pages.takeaway: A safe, explained, and systematic examination comes before individual examination techniques.

pages.title: Inspection
pages.intro: Inspect the patient from the end of the bed and then examine the chest directly. Look for respiratory distress before focusing on anatomical details.

blocks.title: What to assess
items: Respiratory rate, rhythm, and depth.
Use of accessory muscles, recession, or pursed-lip breathing.
Chest shape, symmetry, and movement.
Scars, deformities, or visible lesions.
Cyanosis and relevant signs such as clubbing.

blocks.label: EXAM PEARL
blocks.text: Assess the patient's general appearance and work of breathing before beginning hands-on examination.

images.title: Chest inspection landmarks
images.alt: Placeholder for a diagram showing anterior and posterior chest inspection landmarks
images.caption: Add an anterior and posterior chest landmark diagram.
images.explanation: Use a consistent sequence and compare both sides. Record abnormal shape, asymmetrical movement, scars, and signs of increased work of breathing.

pages.takeaway: Inspection begins before contact and may reveal urgent respiratory compromise.

pages.title: Palpation and chest expansion
pages.intro: Palpation assesses tracheal position, chest expansion, and tactile vocal fremitus when indicated.

blocks.title: Technique
items: Assess tracheal position gently when clinically appropriate.
Place both hands symmetrically on the lower posterior chest.
Position the thumbs near the midline and ask the patient to take a deep breath.
Observe and compare the separation of the thumbs.
If indicated, compare tactile vocal fremitus in symmetrical areas.

blocks.title: Interpretation
blocks.text: Reduced expansion on one side may occur with pleural effusion, pneumothorax, collapse, or other unilateral pathology. Interpret the finding with the history and the rest of the examination.

images.title: Assessing chest expansion
images.alt: Placeholder for a photograph demonstrating hand placement for posterior chest expansion
images.caption: Insert a practical image showing symmetric hand placement on the lower posterior chest.
images.explanation: Place the hands at the same level on each side. The thumbs should move apart symmetrically during inspiration; reduced or asymmetric movement should be documented.

pages.takeaway: Correct hand placement and side-to-side comparison are essential for a reproducible assessment.

pages.title: Percussion
pages.intro: Percussion compares the resonance of underlying lung fields and helps identify areas that may contain air, fluid, or consolidated tissue.

blocks.title: Technique
items: Percuss corresponding areas on the right and left sides.
Use the middle finger of the non-dominant hand as the pleximeter finger.
Strike the finger joint with the tip of the dominant middle finger using a quick wrist movement.
Avoid percussing directly over the scapulae or other bony structures.
Compare percussion notes systematically from apex to base.

blocks.title: Common percussion notes
rows: May occur with consolidation or pleural fluid
May occur with increased air, such as pneumothorax

images.title: Percussion hand technique
images.alt: Placeholder for an image showing correct finger placement during chest percussion
images.caption: Add a close-up image of the pleximeter finger and striking finger.
images.explanation: Keep the pleximeter finger firmly against an intercostal space and lift adjacent fingers away from the chest. Compare like-for-like areas on both sides.

pages.takeaway: A percussion note is one component of the examination and should not be interpreted in isolation.

pages.title: Auscultation
pages.intro: Auscultation evaluates breath sounds and additional sounds. Ask the patient to breathe through an open mouth and listen to a full respiratory cycle at each site.

blocks.title: Technique and findings
items: Warm the stethoscope and place the diaphragm directly on the skin.
Listen systematically over anterior, lateral, and posterior lung fields.
Compare equivalent sites on both sides.
Assess breath-sound intensity and character.
Identify added sounds such as crackles, wheeze, or a pleural rub.
If needed, assess vocal resonance using a consistent phrase.

blocks.label: EXAM PEARL
blocks.text: Ask the patient to take comfortable deep breaths and pause if they become dizzy or uncomfortable.

images.title: Auscultation sites
images.alt: Placeholder for a diagram of anterior and posterior lung auscultation sites
images.caption: Insert a diagram showing a systematic sequence of stethoscope positions.
images.explanation: Listen in a ladder pattern, comparing right and left at each level. Avoid placing the stethoscope over clothing, the scapulae, or other bony areas.

pages.takeaway: Document where abnormal sounds are heard, whether they change with coughing, and how they relate to other findings.

exam.question: During chest expansion assessment, what is the most important comparison?
options: The patient's left and right sides at the same level
The upper chest on one side against the lower chest on the other
The patient's chest against the examiner's chest
exam.explanation: Symmetric hand placement and comparison of both sides during inspiration help identify reduced or unequal expansion.

exam.question: Which percussion note may be associated with pleural effusion?
exam.explanation: Pleural fluid can produce dullness to percussion. Correlate this with examination findings and appropriate investigations.

exam.question: What is the best technique during lung auscultation?
options: Compare equivalent sites on both sides for a full respiratory cycle
Ask the patient to hold their breath at every site
exam.explanation: Systematic side-to-side comparison over a full respiratory cycle improves detection and localization of abnormal breath sounds.
